slides.title: Sensor Registration: Procurement and Build
slides.subtitle: The board, its adapter and the fixtures needed for the registration captures
slides.notes: This is the first of two decks on the registration captures, the session that gathers the sample set for registering the 3D sensor to the robot from plane-to-plane correspondences. It covers what has to exist before a capture session: the flat board, its adapter on the robot flange, the run-out fixture and the measuring tools, with estimated costs and candidate suppliers. Almost all of it is the stage-1 calibration hardware reused; the deck says what to check rather than what to make, and carries the specifications so that the items can be made if stage 1 has not been run. The second deck covers the test procedure itself and what the robot program must do. Both summarize the registration capture procedure in docs/procedures of the plane_plane_registration repository, whose section 1 and appendices A and D hold the full details.

slides.title: One flat board carries the known geometry
slides.caption: The board's front face as the sensor sees it: the tool frame at the center, the four places where D is measured, and the three-point mounting behind it.

cards.head: Board
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm plate, at least 6 mm thick, matte light gray, flat to 0.05 mm after painting and mounting

cards.head: Board adapter
cards.text: Doweled plate on the ISO flange; three support pads, three edge pins, three clamp fingers hold the board square to the flange axis

cards.head: Tool frame
cards.text: Origin at the center of the front face, z along the board normal toward the sensor, x along the long edge; the robot reports this frame

slides.notes: Registration needs only one target: a flat board whose plane the sensor can measure and whose pose the robot reports. The sensor fits a plane to the board in each capture; the robot's reported tool frame gives the same plane in the robot's base frame; the transform that maps one set of planes onto the other is the registration. No spheres and no three-ball nest are needed, which is why this deck is short. The board, its adapter and its tool frame are the stage-1 ones (procedure section 1a and section 3, figure 1). The front face is what matters: its flatness, its matte finish and the perpendicularity of its mounting on the flange axis.

slides.title: What must be built

rows: Board adapter: flange plate with pads, edge pins and clamp fingers
Run-out fixture: dial indicator on a magnetic base and steel base plate

slides.caption: Nothing new if stage 1 was run. Section 1b of the procedure; each item is listed with its specification and drawing so it can be made for this procedure alone.
slides.notes: This is the complete list of apparatus the session needs beyond the sensor, the robot and the computers, as section 1b of the procedure gives it. Every item was built for the stage-1 calibration session and is reused as it is: the same board, the same adapter, the same run-out fixture, the same sensor mount. If stage 1 has not been run, the items are built to the stage-1 specification and drawing, which the procedure carries: the plate specification in section 1d, the run-out fixture in 1e, and drawing SC1-05 for the board adapter in appendix D, copied from the stage-1 repository. The rigid sensor mount is built from the existing drawing from previous work and is not drawn again.

slides.title: What must be bought

rows: Board flatness after painting and mounting
Room temperature in the session notes
Board x axis against the adapter
Isopropyl alcohol and wipes, shim stock

slides.caption: A phone camera is enough for the setup photos. Already in hand: sensor, robot, capture computer with its communication software, analysis computer.
slides.notes: These are the measuring tools and consumables of section 1c of the procedure. All of the tools were bought for stage 1; only consumables are new. The calipers measure the flange-to-face distance D and the board size that go in the pose log; the straightedge and a 0.05 mm feeler leaf check the board's flatness after painting and after mounting; the square sets the board's x axis when the tool frame is defined; the thermometer gives the room temperature for the session notes. No micrometers are needed, since there are no spheres to measure. The sensor, the robot, the capture computer with its communication software and the analysis computer are already in hand (section 1a).

They come from suppliers' list prices where these exist and from typical United States job-shop rates of about 80 to 150 dollars an hour otherwise. If the stage-1 session has been run, the board, the adapter, the run-out fixture and the tools exist, and the only new spending is consumables. Built from nothing, the three items come to 540 to 1,570 dollars and the tools to 170 to 570 dollars. Treat every figure as plus or minus 50 percent and get quotes; the board adapter, a one-off machined plate with lapped pads, is the least certain.

slides.title: Purchase specification: flat plate

rows: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick
Finish-ground aluminum tooling plate (for example MIC-6) or float glass
0.05 mm over the front face, checked with a straightedge and a 0.05 mm feeler leaf after painting and after mounting
Thin, even matte light-gray paint; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm
Bottom long edge and left short edge square and clean: they rest on the adapter's edge pins
Supplier's flatness report, kept with the session notes

slides.caption: Procedure section 1d; the board outline is on drawing SC1-05.
slides.notes: This is the purchase specification of section 1d of the procedure, identical to the stage-1 plate, to hand to a supplier or a grinding shop. The board is checked flat after painting and after mounting because that is the state the sensor sees. Thickness is not a stiffness matter: a 6 mm plate sags only about 0.002 mm under its own weight; the plate only has to survive the finish and the mounting flat. Bead-blasting is ruled out below about 10 mm because peening one face bows the plate; a thin, even matte paint over the ground or glass surface is the finish. The two reference edges rest against the adapter's edge pins, so they must be square and clean.

rows: McMaster-Carr MIC-6 plus a grinding shop; Edmund Optics float glass

Mitutoyo 2046 series; Noga MG71003 or DG-61003
For the run-out fixture; McMaster-Carr and the usual tool suppliers
Mitutoyo or Starrett; DIN 874 grade 0 straightedge
Board adapter and run-out base plate
Drawing SC1-05; the base plate is a plain drilled plate

slides.caption: From suppliers' web pages, October 2026; not an endorsement. Confirm flatness, finish and price before ordering.
slides.notes: This is appendix A of the procedure in brief, the stage-1 supplier list reduced to the items this procedure uses. The plate is one of the two materials of the specification on the previous slide: MIC-6 tooling plate is sold with a stated flatness of about 0.13 mm, coarser than the 0.05 mm asked for, so it is ordered oversize and finish-ground by a local shop; float glass is flat enough as delivered and is the better choice where no grinding shop is at hand. In both cases the supplier's or grinding shop's flatness report is the starting document, and the 0.05 mm is confirmed in-house with the straightedge and feeler leaf after painting and after mounting, the state the sensor sees. The instruments are stock items. The adapter is a one-off job for a machine shop, built to drawing SC1-05.

slides.title: Run-out fixture: indicator and mounting

cards.head: Dial indicator
cards.text: 0.01 mm graduation, about 10 mm travel; for example Mitutoyo 2046 series, about $50 to $150

cards.head: Magnetic base
cards.text: Articulating, with fine adjustment; for example Noga MG71003 or DG-61003, about $140 to $320

cards.head: Steel base plate
cards.text: About 150 x 100 x 12 mm, bolted to the cell table with two M8 screws, so the base holds on any table and does not creep

cards.head: Placement
cards.text: Where the indicator tip reaches the board's front face about 20 mm from an edge with the robot in its run-out pose

slides.caption: The run-out check: joint 6 turns the flange, the indicator stays still, the reading must stay within 0.05 mm.
slides.notes: The run-out check in deck 2 needs the dial indicator held still while the robot turns the board about the flange axis; it tests whether the board face is perpendicular to that axis, which the tool frame's z axis assumes. A magnetic base alone can creep on a non-magnetic table, so the fixture stands on a steel plate bolted down. The stage-1 fixture serves as it is; section 1e of the procedure gives the parts and their placement. The figure is figure 1a of the procedure: the flange, the adapter and the board in section, with the indicator tip on the front face.

slides.title: Keep the board flat after mounting
slides.caption: The front face: tool frame axes, the path of the indicator tip, the four D places, and the adapter's pads, pins and clamp behind the board.

cards.head: Plate
cards.text: 200 x 150 mm, at least 6 mm thick; ground aluminum tooling plate or float glass

cards.head: Finish
cards.text: Matte light gray paint on the front face; do not bead-blast a plate thinner than about 10 mm, it bows

cards.head: Flatness
cards.text: 0.05 mm, checked after painting and mounting, not before; keep the flatness report

cards.head: Adapter
cards.text: Three support pads, three edge pins and three clamp fingers hold the board square to the flange axis, centered on it, and in the same place after a remount

slides.notes: The adapter is the one machined part. Its three lapped pads define the board plane, its three edge pins locate the board within that plane, and its three clamp fingers hold the board against the pads without bending it, so that a remount puts the board back in the same place. The plane of the pads must be parallel to the adapter's back face, which sits on the robot flange; that is what the run-out check verifies after mounting. Drawing SC1-05 in appendix D of the procedure gives every dimension and tolerance; the drawing is generated in the stage-1 repository and copied here. The figure is figure 1b of the procedure.

slides.title: Checks before the board goes to the robot cell
checklist: Board adapter made to drawing SC1-05, flange interface confirmed against the robot's flange drawing
Board flat to 0.05 mm after painting and after mounting on the adapter; flatness report kept
Front face matte, uniform and free of highlights; reference edges square and clean
Board and adapter weighed for the tool load data
Run-out fixture's base plate bolted to the cell table where the indicator reaches the board
Dowels seated; the board goes back in the same place after a remount
slides.notes: These are the build and preparation checks of sections 1 and 3 of the procedure, gathered in one place. Each protects something the software cannot repair later: a board that is not flat gives plane residuals the registration reads as sensor error; a glossy spot returns a highlight and a bad read; a loose or unseated adapter shifts the board between poses and spoils every pose after it; wrong tool load data shifts every reported pose. The run-out and D measurements themselves are session steps, in deck 2.
